parts.title: Sounds & spelling
parts.description: How Finnish is written and pronounced — the foundation for everything else.

parts.title: First steps
parts.description: Greetings, pronouns, the verb olla, saying no, asking questions and counting.

parts.title: Nouns & cases
parts.description: How nouns change: stems, the genitive, 'I have', the partitive, plurals, adjectives and consonant gradation.

parts.title: Verbs
parts.description: The six verb types, consonant gradation in verbs, the imperative and useful verb patterns.

parts.title: Places & movement
parts.description: The six local cases (in, out of, into, on, off, onto), which places take which, verbs of movement and postpositions.

parts.title: Time & everyday life
parts.description: Telling the time, days and dates, months and seasons, and talking about the weather.

topics.title: Alphabet & pronunciation
topics.summary: Finnish is written almost exactly as it is spoken: one letter = one sound, and every letter is pronounced.

sections.heading: The golden rule
sections.body: Each letter always stands for the same sound, and **every letter is pronounced** — there are no silent letters. If you can read a word aloud letter by letter, you can pronounce it. The reverse is also true: if you hear a word clearly, you can spell it.

examples.en: house — t-a-l-o
coffee — the h is pronounced
kitchen — k-e-i-t-t-i-ö

sections.heading: The alphabet (aakkoset)
sections.body: The Finnish alphabet has 29 letters. Native words use only 21 of them; b, c, f, g (except in ng), q, š, w, x, z and å appear in loanwords and names.

sections.heading: Vowels
sections.body: Finnish has eight vowels. Keep them pure — don't glide them into diphthongs like English does.

rows: German ü / French u: say 'ee' with rounded lips
German ö / 'ur' in 'fur' without the r

sections.tip: ä and a are different letters, not accents: **sää** (weather) vs **saa** (gets), **pää** (head) vs **paa**. The same goes for ö/o and y/u.

sections.heading: Consonants to watch
bullets: **r** is always rolled (trilled), even at the end of a word: *kirja*, *tytär*.
**h** is always pronounced, also before a consonant: *kahvi*, *lähteä*, *tehdä*.
**j** sounds like English y: *joulu* ≈ 'youlu', *jäätelö*.
**k, p, t** are unaspirated — softer than in English, no puff of air.
**ng** is a long 'ng' as in 'singer' (never 'finger'): *kengät*, *Helsingissä*.
**nk** is pronounced ŋk as in 'bank': *Helsinki*, *pankki*.
**s** is always a sharp s (never z): *vesi*, *Suomi*.

sections.heading: Spelling letter by letter
sections.body: When you spell a name on the phone, say the letter names from the table above. Useful phrases: **Miten se kirjoitetaan?** (How is it written?) — **Voitko tavata sen?** (Can you spell it?).

examples.fi: Mikä sinun nimesi on? — Gavin. G-A-V-I-N.
examples.en: What's your name? — Gavin. gee-aa-vee-ii-än.

topics.title: Long and short sounds
topics.summary: A doubled letter is a longer sound — and length changes the meaning of the word.

sections.heading: Length is meaning
sections.body: Every vowel and most consonants can be short (one letter) or long (two letters). A long sound is held roughly twice as long. Getting the length wrong gives you a different word, so practise hearing it.

sections.heading: How to pronounce long consonants
sections.body: A double consonant (**kk, pp, tt, ss, ll, mm, nn, rr**) is a real pause/hold in the middle of the word, belonging to both syllables: *kis-sa*, *mat-to*, *kauppa* (kaup-pa). Think of the gap in English 'black cat' or 'hot tea'.

examples.en: fire / wind / customs
but / other (partitive)
who / flower
back- / fireplace
piece / burns / ball
weather / gets (vowel quality, not length)
style / calm

sections.heading: Why it matters for grammar
sections.body: Length is also how grammar works: the hän form of a type 1 verb lengthens the last vowel (*puhu-* → **puhuu**), the illative case lengthens the vowel (*talo* → **taloon**), and K-P-T gradation turns long consonants short (*kauppa* → *kaupassa*). See [[kpt-nouns|Consonant gradation in nouns]] and [[kpt-verbs|K-P-T in verbs]].

topics.title: Stress & diphthongs
topics.summary: Stress always falls on the first syllable. Two different vowels side by side often glide together into one syllable (a diphthong).

sections.heading: Stress: always the first syllable
sections.body: The main stress is **always on the first syllable**, no matter how long the word is. In long words there is a lighter secondary stress on the 3rd or 5th syllable. Long vowels in later syllables are *not* stressed — they are just long.

examples.en: Finland
Helsinki
restaurant
in the shop
into the house (long oo, stress still on ta-)

sections.heading: Diphthongs
sections.body: A diphthong is two different vowels pronounced in one syllable, gliding from the first to the second. Pronounce both vowels clearly.

rows: ai, ei, oi, ui, yi, äi, öi
kaikki, hei, poika, uida, äiti, öisin
au, eu, iu, ou / äy, öy
auto, Eurooppa, kiuas, Oulu / käydä, löytää

sections.note: ie, uo and yö are only diphthongs in the first syllable; elsewhere the two vowels belong to separate syllables: *ra-di-o*, *tor-ni-en*.

examples.en: night — work — (district of Helsinki)
road — language — to take
swamp — Finland — to drink
mother — to visit — table

topics.title: Vowel harmony
topics.summary: Endings come in two flavours — -a/-o/-u for 'back' words and -ä/-ö/-y for 'front' words. The word itself decides which one you use.

rows: go with either; a word with only e/i takes front endings

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Look at the word: **if it contains a, o or u anywhere, use the back endings; otherwise use the front endings.** (In compound words, the last part decides: *jää|kaappi* → *jääkaapissa*.)

sections.heading: Where you meet it
bullets: Case endings: -ssa/-ssä, -sta/-stä, -lla/-llä, -lta/-ltä, -a/-ä, -ta/-tä.
Question suffix: Onko? — Ei**kö**? — Puhut**ko**? — Syöt**kö**?
Verb endings: puhu**vat** — syö**vät**; the infinitive: puhu**a** — kysy**ä**.
Imperative plural: puhu**kaa** — syö**kää**.

examples.en: I live in London. I work in the kitchen.
Do you speak Finnish? — Do you eat fish?
They speak. — They ask.

topics.title: Greetings & polite phrases
topics.summary: Hello, goodbye, how are you, thank you — and which greeting fits which time of day.

sections.heading: Hello & goodbye

rows: any time, informal (moi is very common)

sections.tip: **Hyvää** is the partitive of *hyvä* (good): greetings are short wishes — 'good day (to you)'.

rows: Hyvää, kiitos. Entä sinulle? — Fine, thanks. And you?
Hyvin! / Ihan hyvin. / Ei hassummin. / Huonosti.
Kuinka voit? — How are you feeling?
Here you are / You're welcome (sg. / pl. & polite)
Mikä sinun nimesi on? — Minun nimeni on …
What's your name? — My name is …
Mistä sinä olet kotoisin? — Olen kotoisin Englannista.
Where are you from? — I'm from England.

topics.title: Personal pronouns
topics.summary: minä, sinä, hän, me, te, he — and Finnish has no 'he' vs 'she'.

sections.heading: The six persons
bullets: **hän** covers both he and she — no grammatical gender anywhere in Finnish.
**te** is also the polite 'you' for one person (teititellä), e.g. with older strangers or in formal letters.
Because the verb ending shows the person, **minä, sinä, me, te are often dropped**: *(Minä) Asun Lontoossa.* — but **hän** and **he** are always kept.

sections.heading: Pronoun forms you will meet early
sections.note: See [[genitive|Genitive]], [[have-adessive|Minulla on]] and [[partitive|Partitive]].

topics.title: The verb olla — to be
topics.summary: olen, olet, on, olemme, olette, ovat — the most important (and irregular) verb.

examples.en: I am Gavin. I am English.
He/she is a teacher.
We are at home.
You are Finnish (pl. → partitive plural).

examples.fi: Tämä on kirja. Kirja on punainen.
examples.en: This is a book. The book is red.
It is three o'clock.
Today is Monday.
It is cold outside (no 'it' in Finnish).

sections.heading: Good to know
bullets: There is **no word for 'a/an' or 'the'**: *Hän on opettaja* = he is a teacher.
With weather, time and temperature there is no subject: *On kylmä.* (It's cold.) *Sataa.* (It's raining.)
**olla + adessive** = to have: *Minulla on koira.* (see [[have-adessive|Minulla on]])
Spoken Finnish: mä oon, sä oot, se on, me ollaan, te ootte, ne on.

topics.title: Saying no: the negative verb
topics.summary: Finnish says 'no' with a verb of its own: en, et, ei, emme, ette, eivät + the verb's stem.

sections.heading: The negative verb changes, the main verb doesn't
sections.body: In a negative sentence the **person ending moves to the negative verb** *e-*, and the main verb loses its ending (it takes the same stem as the minä form, without -n).

sections.heading: How to make it
bullets: Take the **minä** form and remove **-n**: puhun → *puhu*, nukun → *nuku*, tapaan → *tapaa*.
Put the right form of **e-** in front: *en puhu, ei nuku, emme tapaa*.
Type 1 verbs with K-P-T keep the **weak** grade in all negative forms: *hän nukkuu* → *hän ei nuku* (see [[kpt-verbs|K-P-T in verbs]]).

sections.heading: Negation changes the object to partitive
sections.body: In a negative sentence the object (and the 'thing you have') goes into the **partitive**:

examples.fi: Minulla on auto. → Minulla ei ole autoa.
examples.en: I have a car. → I don't have a car.
I'll buy the book. → I won't buy a book.
He/she doesn't drink coffee.

sections.heading: Short answers

examples.en: Are you Finnish? — No (I'm not). / Yes (I am).
Do you speak Swedish? — No.

examples.fi: Asuuko hän Helsingissä? — Ei asu. / Asuu.
examples.en: Does he live in Helsinki? — No. / Yes.

sections.tip: Finns answer yes/no questions by **repeating the verb**: *Puhutko englantia? — Puhun.* A plain *kyllä/joo* or *ei* is also fine.

topics.title: Yes/no questions with -ko/-kö
topics.summary: Add -ko or -kö to the verb and move it to the front: Puhut suomea → Puhutko suomea?

sections.heading: How to build a yes/no question
bullets: Take the verb and add **-ko** (back-vowel words) or **-kö** (front-vowel words) — see [[vowel-harmony|vowel harmony]].
Put the verb **first** in the sentence.
No 'do/does' is needed.

sections.heading: Negative questions
sections.body: Add -kö to the negative verb (always -kö, because e- is a front word): **enkö, etkö, eikö, emmekö, ettekö, eivätkö**.

examples.en: Don't you speak Finnish?
Isn't he/she at home?

sections.heading: Focusing other words
sections.body: -ko/-kö can be attached to any word you want to question; that word goes first.

examples.en: Is it tomorrow that you're coming?
Is it coffee you're drinking?

topics.title: Question words
topics.summary: Mikä, kuka, missä, mistä, mihin, milloin, miten… Most question words are forms of mikä (what) and kuka (who).

rows: Mikä tämä on? — What is this?
Mitä sinä teet? — What are you doing?
Kuka hän on? — Who is he/she?
Kenen kirja tämä on? — Whose book is this?
Kenellä on avain? — Who has the key?
Missä sinä asut? — Where do you live?
Mistä sinä olet kotoisin? — Where are you from?
Mihin sinä menet? — Where are you going?
Milloin kurssi alkaa? — When does the course start?
Mitä kello on? / Paljonko kello on?
Miksi opiskelet suomea? — Why are you studying Finnish?
Paljonko tämä maksaa? — How much does this cost?
Millainen sää on tänään? — What's the weather like?

sections.heading: Missä — mistä — mihin
sections.body: The three 'where' words match the three directions of the [[local-cases|local cases]]. Always answer in the same direction:

examples.en: Where are you? — I'm in the shop.
Where are you coming from? — From the shop.
Where are you going? — To the shop.

sections.heading: Tip
sections.body: No -ko/-kö is added when the sentence already has a question word: *Missä sinä asut?* (not ✗*Missäkö*).

topics.title: Numbers
topics.summary: yksi, kaksi, kolme… Teens add -toista, tens add kymmentä, and the thing you count goes into the partitive.

sections.heading: Tens, hundreds, thousands
sections.body: Multiply with **kymmentä** (tens), **sataa** (hundreds), **tuhatta** (thousands) — these are partitive forms. Just write the parts one after the other (as one word up to 999).

sections.heading: Counting things: number + partitive
sections.body: After every number except *yksi* (1) the noun goes into the **partitive singular** — never plural.

examples.en: one cat — two cats
three children (lapsi → lasta)
five euros
twenty degrees

examples.fi: Minulla on kaksi veljeä ja yksi sisko.
examples.en: I have two brothers and one sister.

sections.note: See [[partitive|Partitive]].

sections.heading: Ordinal numbers (1st, 2nd…)
sections.body: Used for dates and floors. Written with a full stop: 1. = ensimmäinen.

examples.en: I live on the third floor.

examples.fi: Paljonko tämä maksaa? — Se maksaa kolme euroa viisikymmentä (senttiä).
examples.en: How much is this? — It costs €3.50.

examples.fi: Puhelinnumeroni on nolla neljä nolla, yksi kaksi kolme…
examples.en: My phone number is 040 123… (digits one by one)

topics.title: Countries, nationalities & languages
topics.summary: Suomi → suomalainen → suomi (the language). Nationalities end in -lainen/-läinen; languages and nationalities are written with a small letter.

sections.heading: Rules
bullets: Nationality = country (or its stem) + **-lainen** (back words) / **-läinen** (front words): *Venäjä → venäläinen*.
Countries are capitalised; **nationalities and languages are not**: *Suomi* but *suomalainen*, *suomi*.
'I speak X' uses the **partitive**: *Puhun suomea, englantia ja vähän ruotsia.*
Plural of -nen words: *suomalainen → suomalaiset* (we are Finns: *Me olemme suomalaisia*).

examples.fi: Mistä sinä olet kotoisin? — Olen kotoisin Englannista.
examples.en: Where are you from? — I'm from England.

examples.fi: Hän on Ruotsista, mutta asuu Suomessa.
examples.en: He/she is from Sweden but lives in Finland.

topics.title: Noun stems: what happens before an ending
topics.summary: Before you add a case ending, many words change shape. A handful of patterns covers almost every word you'll meet.

sections.heading: Why stems matter
sections.body: Finnish has about 15 cases, but they all attach to the same **stem**. If you know the genitive (-n form) of a word, you know its stem: just remove the -n. *talon → talo-*, *huoneen → huonee-*, *naisen → naise-*.
sections.tip: When you learn a new noun, learn it as a pair: **basic form + genitive** (talo, talon · kieli, kielen · huone, huoneen).

sections.heading: The main patterns

rows: a, o, u, y, ä, ö

sections.note: Old -i words (kieli, ovi, järvi, lumi, nimi, uni, tuli, meri, pilvi, lehti…) must simply be learnt. New words and loans (kahvi, banaani, pankki, bussi, hotelli) keep the i.

sections.heading: Plus consonant gradation
sections.body: On top of the stem change, many words switch between a strong and weak consonant (kauppa → kaupassa, katu → kadulla). See [[kpt-nouns|Consonant gradation in nouns]].

topics.title: Genitive -n (of, 's)
topics.summary: The genitive ends in -n and means 'of' or 's: Pekan auto (Pekka's car), Suomen pääkaupunki (the capital of Finland).

sections.heading: Formation
sections.body: Stem + **-n**. Watch the stem (see [[word-stems|Noun stems]]) and K-P-T gradation (the -n closes the syllable, so the weak grade appears).

sections.heading: Uses
bullets: **Possession**: *Liisan koira* — Liisa's dog; *minun äitini* — my mother.
**'of'**: *Suomen pääkaupunki* — the capital of Finland; *talon katto* — the roof of the house.
**Before postpositions**: *talon edessä* — in front of the house; *pöydän alla* — under the table (see [[postpositions|Postpositions]]).
**'Whose?'** = *Kenen?*: *Kenen kirja tämä on? — Se on Annan kirja.*
**Total object** (a whole, finished thing): *Ostan auton.* — I (will) buy a/the car (see [[object-case|Object]]).

examples.en: My father's name is Juhani.
Pekka's sister lives in Turku.

examples.fi: Kenen laukku tämä on? — Se on opettajan laukku.
examples.en: Whose bag is this? — It's the teacher's bag.

examples.fi: Suomen lippu on sininen ja valkoinen.
examples.en: Finland's flag is blue and white.

sections.heading: Plural genitive (for recognition)
sections.body: The plural genitive usually ends in **-den/-tten** or **-jen/-ien**: *talojen* (of the houses), *naisten* (of the women), *lasten* (of the children). You'll meet it in set phrases: *lasten huone* (children's room).

topics.title: My, your, his — possessives
topics.summary: minun kirja(ni), sinun kirja(si)… Possession is shown with a genitive pronoun and (in written Finnish) a possessive suffix.

sections.heading: The full pattern
bullets: The suffixes are **-ni, -si, -nsa/-nsä, -mme, -nne, -nsa/-nsä**.
With *minä, sinä, me, te* the pronoun can be dropped: *Kirjani on tässä.* (My book is here.)
Before a suffix the word takes its stem + weak/strong grade as in the genitive: *äiti → äitini*, *nimi → nimeni*, *huone → huoneeni*.
In everyday speech and in this course you can safely say **minun kirja** / **mun kirja**; recognise the suffixes when you read.

examples.fi: Mikä sinun nimesi on? — Minun nimeni on Gavin.
examples.en: What's your name? — My name is Gavin.
This is my family.
His/her son is a teacher.
Our house is old.

examples.fi: Kenen tämä puhelin on? — Se on minun.
examples.en: Whose phone is this? — It's mine.

examples.fi: Onko tämä sinun? — Ei, se on Pekan.
examples.en: Is this yours? — No, it's Pekka's.

topics.title: To have: minulla on
topics.summary: Finnish has no verb 'to have'. Instead: 'at me is' — Minulla on koira (I have a dog).

sections.heading: The structure: owner in -lla/-llä + on + thing
bullets: The verb is **always on** (3rd person singular) — even with *meillä* or *heillä*, even with plural things.
The owner goes into the **adessive** (-lla/-llä): *äiti → äidillä*, *Anna → Annalla*, *opettaja → opettajalla*.
Negative: **ei ole** + thing in the **partitive**: *Minulla ei ole autoa.*

examples.en: I have two children.

examples.fi: Onko sinulla sisaruksia? — On, minulla on yksi veli.
examples.en: Do you have siblings? — Yes, I have one brother.

examples.fi: Meillä ei ole koiraa, mutta meillä on kissa.
examples.en: We don't have a dog, but we have a cat.

examples.fi: Hänellä on siniset silmät ja pitkä tukka.
examples.en: He/she has blue eyes and long hair.

examples.fi: Minulla on nälkä / jano / kylmä / kuuma.
examples.en: I'm hungry / thirsty / cold / hot.

examples.fi: Minulla on flunssa. Minulla on päänsärky.
examples.en: I have the flu. I have a headache.
I'm in a hurry.

sections.heading: Answering

examples.fi: Onko sinulla lemmikkiä? — On. / Ei ole.
examples.en: Do you have a pet? — Yes. / No.

sections.tip: Questions with 'onko … ?' often use the partitive for things you'd count: *Onko sinulla lapsia?* (any children?).

topics.title: Partitive singular
topics.summary: The partitive (-a/-ä, -ta/-tä, -tta/-ttä) is the 'some / part of / not whole' case — used after numbers, in negative sentences, for uncountables and with many verbs.

sections.heading: Endings — the rules from the course

rows: one short vowel (talo, kissa, kahvi, omena, leipä)
long vowel or diphthong (maa, tee, puu, tie)

sections.note: The partitive keeps the same grade as the basic form: *kauppa → kauppaa*, *äiti → äitiä* (strong), but *sade → sadetta*, *opas → opasta* (weak).

sections.heading: When to use it
bullets: **After numbers (2+)** and quantity words: *kaksi kahvia*, *paljon lunta*, *vähän rahaa*, *kilo omenoita*.
**Negative sentences**: *Minulla ei ole autoa.* *En juo kahvia.*
**Uncountable things** (mass nouns) — some, an amount: *Juon vettä.* *Ostan maitoa ja leipää.*
**Ongoing / unfinished action** and verbs that always take it: *rakastaa, odottaa, auttaa, ajatella, katsoa (TV), kuunnella, opiskella, harrastaa*: *Rakastan sinua. Odotan bussia. Opiskelen suomea.*
**Languages you speak**: *Puhun suomea.*
**Questions about having**: *Onko sinulla lapsia?*
**Describing uncountable subjects**: *Kahvi on kuumaa.* (the coffee is hot — material/mass)
**Greetings and wishes**: *Hyvää huomenta! Hyvää joulua!*

examples.fi: Saanko kupin kahvia ja palan kakkua?
examples.en: Can I have a cup of coffee and a piece of cake?
I'd like (some) tea and two buns.
Do you have gluten-free bread?
No thanks, I don't drink milk.

topics.title: Plural: -t
topics.summary: The basic plural is stem + -t: talo → talot, kauppa → kaupat, huone → huoneet.

sections.heading: Nominative plural
sections.body: Take the genitive singular and replace **-n with -t**. So the stem and weak grade are the same as in the genitive.

sections.heading: When to use the -t plural
bullets: Specific, whole groups as subject: *Lapset leikkivät pihalla.* — The children are playing in the yard.

Things that come in pairs or sets are often plural in Finnish: *housut* (trousers), *farkut* (jeans), *sakset* (scissors), *silmälasit* (glasses), *häät* (wedding), *juhlat* (party), *synttärit* (birthday party).
Adjectives agree: *siniset silmät* (blue eyes), *mustat kengät* (black shoes).
After numbers you still use the **singular partitive**: *kaksi taloa* (not ✗taloja).

sections.heading: Plural in other cases (for recognition)
sections.body: Inside the plural, the marker is **-i-** (or -j- between vowels): *taloissa* (in the houses), *kaupoissa*, *kaduilla*, *huoneissa*. A short vowel before -i- often changes: a → o/–, ä → –, e → –: *kauppa → kaupoissa*, *kissa → kissoilla*, *päivä → päivinä*.

topics.title: Partitive plural
topics.summary: Some / many of a countable thing: omenoita (apples), kirjoja (books), lapsia (children).

sections.heading: Endings
sections.note: *kukka → kukkia is an exception to the o-rule. The partitive plural is one of the trickiest forms — learn the common ones as vocabulary: lapsia, omenoita, perunoita, mansikoita, kirjoja, kukkia, ystäviä, kenkiä, vaatteita, huoneita, naisia.

sections.heading: When
bullets: Indefinite amount of countable things: *Ostan omenoita.* — I'm buying (some) apples.
Negative and questions with plural meaning: *Onko sinulla lapsia? — Ei, minulla ei ole lapsia.*
After *paljon* (a lot) and *vähän* (a little): *Kaupassa on paljon ihmisiä.* (But *monta* + singular partitive: *monta ihmistä*.)
Plural 'are': *He ovat suomalaisia. Kengät ovat kalliita.*

topics.title: Adjectives, colours & describing people
topics.summary: Adjectives come before the noun and take the same case ending: iso talo → isossa talossa. Millainen hän on? describes people.

sections.heading: Agreement
sections.body: An adjective in front of a noun takes **the same case and number** as the noun.

rows: in front of the big house
The house is big. (no agreement needed after 'on')

sections.heading: Describing people — Millainen hän on?

rows: Hän on pitkä ja hoikka. Hän on iloinen ja ystävällinen.
Hänellä on lyhyt, vaalea tukka ja siniset silmät.
Hän on noin neljäkymmentä vuotta vanha.
Hänellä on päällä punainen takki ja mustat housut.

sections.tip: Appearance with 'have': *hänellä on* + plural nominative: *siniset silmät*, *pitkät hiukset*. Height and build with 'is': *hän on pitkä / lyhyt / hoikka / tukeva*.

sections.heading: Colours — Minkä värinen?

examples.fi: Minkä värinen sinun autosi on? — Se on punainen.
examples.en: What colour is your car? — It's red.
light blue / dark blue (vaalea- light, tumma- dark)

sections.note: Colours ending in -nen inflect like *nainen*: *punaisessa talossa*, *punaista*, *punaiset*.

topics.title: Consonant gradation in nouns (K-P-T)
topics.summary: k, p and t change when a syllable closes: kauppa → kaupassa, katu → kadulla, Helsinki → Helsingissä.

sections.heading: Strong and weak grade
sections.body: The consonants **k, p, t** in the last syllable of a word have a *strong* and a *weak* form. Which one you use depends on whether the **syllable is open or closed** after the ending is added.
bullets: Open syllable (ends in a vowel) → **strong**: *kaup-pa*, *ka-tu*.
Closed syllable (ends in a consonant, e.g. -n, -t, -ssa, -lla) → **weak**: *kau-pan*, *ka-dun*, *kau-pas-sa*, *ka-dul-la*.
For basic-form words that end in a vowel, the basic form is strong and most endings make it weak.

rows: katu → kadulla, äiti → äidin, pöytä → pöydällä

sections.heading: Which endings make it weak?
sections.tip: Memory hook: the **partitive, illative and essive** keep the strong grade (their ending starts a new open syllable or lengthens the vowel); almost everything else is weak.

sections.heading: Reverse gradation: -e words
sections.body: Words ending in **-e** (and many in -as, -is, -in) work the other way round: the basic form is **weak** and the inflected forms are **strong**: **sade → sateen** (rain), **koe → kokeen** (test), **opas → oppaan** (guide), **rikas → rikkaan** (rich), **hammas → hampaan** (tooth), **lammas → lampaan** (sheep), **soitin → soittimen** (instrument), **keitin → keittimen** (kettle).
sections.note: The same reverse pattern happens in verb types 3 and 4: see [[kpt-verbs-3-4|K-P-T in verb types 3 & 4]].

sections.heading: Farm animals and food from the course

examples.fi: lehmä → lehmät · lammas → lampaat · vuohi → vuohet
examples.en: cow → cows · sheep → sheep (reverse: mm → mp) · goat → goats

examples.fi: kukko → kukon · porsas → porsaan · pukki → pukin
examples.en: rooster · piglet · billy goat

examples.fi: leipä → leivän · peruna → perunan · liha → lihan
examples.en: bread · potato · meat
I buy bread and tomatoes from the shop.

topics.title: The object: genitive-n, partitive or nominative
topics.summary: A whole, finished object takes -n (Ostan auton); a partial, ongoing or negative one takes the partitive (Ostan maitoa, En osta autoa).

rows: En syö lihaa. — I don't eat meat.
Luen kirjaa. — I'm reading a book (not finished).
Luen kirjan. — I'll read the (whole) book.
Osta leipä! — Buy a loaf! · Syö omena! — Eat an apple!
Ostan liput. — I'll buy the tickets.

sections.heading: Verbs that always take the partitive
sections.body: Some verbs express ongoing feelings or activities and always take a partitive object: **rakastaa** (love), **odottaa** (wait for), **auttaa** (help), **ajatella** (think of), **harrastaa** (have as a hobby), **opiskella** (study), **soittaa** (play an instrument), **kuunnella** (listen to), **katsoa** (watch).

examples.en: I'm waiting for the bus.
My hobbies are yoga and skiing.
I play the guitar.

topics.title: The six verb types — overview
topics.summary: Every Finnish verb belongs to one of six types, recognised from the end of the infinitive. The type tells you how to find the stem.

sections.heading: Personal endings are the same for every verb
sections.body: What differs between the types is only **how you get the stem** from the infinitive.

sections.heading: How to recognise the type
sections.tip: Check the **last two letters** first: -da/-dä → type 2; double consonant or -st- + a → type 3; vowel + a → type 1; t + a after a vowel → 4, 5 or 6 (look at the vowel before -ta).

sections.heading: Which types have K-P-T?
bullets: **Type 1**: infinitive is strong → minä, sinä, me, te and the negative are **weak** (*nukkua → nukun*). See [[kpt-verbs|K-P-T in verb type 1]].
**Type 2**: no gradation.
**Types 3 and 4** (and 6): infinitive is **weak** → all personal forms are **strong** (*ajatella → ajattelen*, *tavata → tapaan*). See [[kpt-verbs-3-4|K-P-T in types 3 & 4]].
**Type 5**: no gradation.

sections.heading: Exceptions worth knowing
bullets: **olla** (to be) — olen, olet, on, olemme, olette, ovat.
**tehdä** (to do/make) — teen, teet, tekee, teemme, teette, tekevät.
**nähdä** (to see) — näen, näet, näkee, näemme, näette, näkevät.
**juosta** (to run) — juoksen, juokset, juoksee…
**maata** (to lie down) — makaan, makaat, makaa…
Some -ita/-eta verbs belong to type 4: **hävitä** → häviän, **kiivetä** → kiipeän, **selvitä** → selviän.

topics.title: Verb type 1 (-a/-ä after a vowel)
topics.summary: The biggest group: puhua, asua, ostaa, lukea… Drop the final -a/-ä to get the stem; hän doubles the last vowel.

sections.heading: Formation
sections.body: Infinitive minus the final **-a/-ä** = stem. Add the personal endings. In the **hän** form the last vowel of the stem doubles (unless it is already long or a diphthong ending in the same vowel).
sections.note: *lukea* shows K-P-T: k disappears in the weak forms (luen, luet). See [[kpt-verbs|K-P-T in verb type 1]].

sections.heading: Common type 1 verbs from the course

examples.en: I live in London and speak English.

examples.fi: Mitä tämä maksaa? — Se maksaa kaksi euroa.
examples.en: How much does this cost? — It costs two euros.
The children are playing in the yard.
We're watching a film in the evening.

topics.title: K-P-T in verb type 1
topics.summary: nukkua → minä nukun, hän nukkuu. In type 1, minä/sinä/me/te and the negative take the weak grade; hän and he stay strong.

sections.heading: The pattern
sections.body: The endings **-n, -t, -mme, -tte** close the syllable → **weak grade**. The hän form (long vowel) and he form (-vat) keep it open → **strong grade**. The negative uses the same stem as minä → **weak**.

sections.heading: All the changes

rows: ottaa, odottaa, kirjoittaa, soittaa, auttaa, muuttaa

sections.note: No gradation after s, or in st, sk, tk, ts: *istua → istun*, *etsiä → etsin*, *tutkia → tutkin*, *katsoa → katson*.

examples.en: I usually sleep eight hours.

examples.fi: Hän lukee kirjaa, mutta minä en lue.
examples.en: He/she is reading a book, but I'm not.
We leave for the cottage on Friday.

examples.fi: Pidän kahvista, mutta en pidä teestä.
examples.en: I like coffee, but I don't like tea.

examples.fi: Tiedätkö, missä asema on? — En tiedä.
examples.en: Do you know where the station is? — I don't know.

topics.title: Verb type 2 (-da/-dä)
topics.summary: syödä, juoda, käydä, tehdä, nähdä… Drop -da/-dä; the hän form is just the stem. No consonant gradation (except tehdä/nähdä).

sections.heading: Formation
bullets: Stem = infinitive minus **-da/-dä**.
**hän**: nothing is added — *hän syö*, *hän juo*.
**tehdä** and **nähdä** are irregular: stem *tee-/näe-*, but *tekee/näkee* and *tekevät/näkevät*.

examples.fi: Syön aamulla puuroa ja juon kahvia.
examples.en: In the morning I eat porridge and drink coffee.
I go to the shop every day.
What are you doing at the weekend?
Can I help? — May I have some coffee?

topics.title: Verb type 3 (-la, -na, -ra, -sta)
topics.summary: tulla → tulen, mennä → menen, nousta → nousen, opiskella → opiskelen. Drop the last two letters and add -e.

sections.heading: Formation
sections.body: Remove the last two letters (**-la/-lä, -na/-nä, -ra/-rä, -ta/-tä**) and add **-e**. hän lengthens it: **-ee**.
sections.note: **juosta** (run) is irregular: *juoksen, juokset, juoksee*. **olla** is technically type 3 but irregular.

examples.en: Are you coming tomorrow? — Yes.
I'm going home by bus.
In winter we skate and ski.
He/she studies Finnish on Mondays.

sections.heading: Reverse K-P-T
sections.body: Some type 3 verbs have a weak grade in the infinitive and a strong grade in all personal forms: *ajatella → ajattelen*, *kuunnella → kuuntelen*. See [[kpt-verbs-3-4|K-P-T in verb types 3 & 4]].

topics.title: Verb type 4 (-ata, -ota, -uta, -ätä…)
topics.summary: haluta → haluan, avata → avaan, pelata → pelaan. Drop -ta and add -a/-ä.

sections.heading: Formation
sections.body: Remove **-ta/-tä** and add **-a/-ä** (so -ata becomes -aa-, -uta becomes -ua-). hän adds another vowel unless there are already two the same (*avaa*, but *haluaa*).

examples.en: Would you like some coffee? — Yes, I would.
The shop opens at nine o'clock.
In winter we play ice hockey.
Can you swim? — Yes, I can.
I wake up at seven o'clock.

sections.heading: Reverse K-P-T
sections.body: When the infinitive has a weak consonant, **every** personal form (including hän and he) is strong: *tavata → tapaan, tapaa, tapaavat*; *pakata → pakkaan*; *hypätä → hyppään*. See [[kpt-verbs-3-4|K-P-T in verb types 3 & 4]].

topics.title: Verb type 5 (-ita/-itä)
topics.summary: tarvita → tarvitsen, valita → valitsen. Drop -a/-ä and add -se.

sections.heading: Formation
sections.body: Remove the final **-a/-ä** and add **-se**; hän: **-see**. No consonant gradation.
sections.note: A few -ita/-itä verbs are actually type 4: *hävitä → häviän* (lose), *selvitä → selviän* (survive), *levitä → leviän* (spread).

examples.en: I need new shoes.
In winter we need warm clothes.
What does this word mean?
Will you choose coffee or tea?

topics.title: Verb type 6 (-eta/-etä)
topics.summary: A small group meaning 'to become …': vanheta → vanhenen (grow old), lämmetä → lämpenee (get warmer).

sections.heading: Formation
sections.body: Remove **-ta/-tä** and add **-ne**; hän: **-nee**. Reverse K-P-T like types 3 and 4 (*lämmetä → lämpenee*).

examples.fi: Syksyllä ilma kylmenee ja illat pimenevät.
examples.en: In autumn the air gets colder and the evenings get darker.
In spring the weather gets warmer.

topics.title: K-P-T in verb types 3 & 4
topics.summary: Reverse gradation: the infinitive is weak, every personal form is strong — tavata → tapaan, tapaa; ajatella → ajattelen, ajattelee.

sections.heading: Why it's 'reverse'
sections.body: In types 3 and 4 the infinitive ends in a closed syllable (*a-ja-tel-la*, *ta-vat-a*), so the infinitive has the **weak** grade. In the personal forms the syllable is open (*a-jat-te-len*, *ta-paan*), so they have the **strong** grade. And because the ending doesn't close anything new, **all six persons and the negative are strong** — unlike type 1, where hän/he differ.

sections.heading: All the changes (weak → strong)

rows: pakata → pakkaan, hakata → hakkaan, leikata → leikkaan
mitata → mittaan, ajatella → ajattelen, jutella → juttelen, esitellä → esittelen, luetella → luettelen
pudota → putoan, kadota → katoan, riidellä → riitelen
tavata → tapaan, luvata → lupaan, kaivata → kaipaan, levätä → lepään

sections.note: Not every v or l alternates: *avata → avaan*, *kävellä → kävelen*, *pelata → pelaan* have no gradation. Watch out for st, sk: *opiskella → opiskelen*, *vastata → vastaan*.

examples.en: I'm meeting my friend at the café.
I'll pack my bag in the evening.

examples.fi: Hän kuuntelee musiikkia ja ajattelee kesää.
examples.en: He/she listens to music and thinks about summer.
The leaves fall from the trees in autumn.
The children jump and run in the yard.

topics.title: Imperative — giving instructions
topics.summary: Tule! (Come!) — Tulkaa! (Come, all of you!) — Älä tule! — Älkää tulko! The singular imperative looks like the minä form without -n.

sections.heading: Singular (to one person, sinä)
sections.body: Take the **minä** form and drop **-n**. It is the same as the negative stem, so K-P-T type 1 verbs are **weak**: *nukkua → nuku!*

sections.heading: Plural / polite (to several people, te)
sections.body: Type 1 and 2: drop -a/-ä or -da/-dä (*puhu-kaa*, *teh-kää*). Type 3: drop the last two letters, -la/-na/-ra/-ta (*tul-kaa*, *men-kää*, *nous-kaa*). Types 4–6: drop the final -a/-ä (*avat-kaa*, *tarvit-kaa*). Then add **-kaa/-kää**. Negative: **älkää** + the same stem + **-ko/-kö**. Type 1 keeps the **strong** grade (*nukkukaa*).
sections.tip: Shortcut: types 4–6 = infinitive minus -a/-ä + kaa (*avata → avat-kaa*); type 3 = infinitive minus its last two letters + kaa (*tulla → tul-kaa*).

sections.heading: Let's …! (me)
sections.body: In spoken Finnish 'let's' is the passive form: **Mennään!** (Let's go!), **Syödään!** (Let's eat!), **Aloitetaan!** (Let's start!). Negative: *Ei mennä!*

sections.heading: The object of an imperative
sections.body: A whole, countable object is in the **basic form** (no -n): *Osta leipä!* (Buy a loaf!), *Avaa ovi!* (Open the door!). Uncountable or negative → partitive: *Osta maitoa! Älä avaa ovea!*

examples.en: Listen! Repeat! Write! (to the class)
Open your books at page ten.

examples.fi: Istu alas! Ole hyvä ja istu.
examples.en: Sit down! Please sit down.

examples.fi: Hengitä sisään… ja ulos. Nosta kädet ylös.
examples.en: Breathe in… and out. Raise your arms. (yoga)
Turn right and go straight on.
Don't forget the keys!
Come here! Wait a moment!

topics.title: Verb patterns: I want to…, I like…
topics.summary: Haluan syödä (I want to eat), Osaan uida (I can swim), Pidän kahvista (I like coffee), Tykkään hiihtää.

sections.heading: Verb + infinitive
sections.body: Many verbs are followed by a second verb in the **infinitive** (dictionary form):

rows: Haluan oppia suomea. — I want to learn Finnish.
Voin tulla huomenna. — I can come tomorrow.
Saanko istua tässä? — May I sit here?
Alkaa sataa. — It's starting to rain.
Yritän puhua suomea. — I try to speak Finnish.
Minun täytyy mennä. — I have to go.

sections.heading: Liking: pitää + elative (-sta/-stä)
sections.body: **pitää** ('to like') takes its object in the **elative**: *pidän kahvista* = I like coffee. (In speech, **tykätä** works the same way: *tykkään kahvista*.)

examples.fi: Pidän suklaasta, mutta en pidä lakritsista.
examples.en: I like chocolate, but I don't like liquorice.

examples.fi: Mistä sinä pidät? — Pidän joogasta ja kävelystä.
examples.en: What do you like? — I like yoga and walking.
Do you like sauna?

topics.title: The six local cases — overview
topics.summary: Where? Where from? Where to? — answered with six endings: -ssa, -sta, -Vn (inside) and -lla, -lta, -lle (on / at).

sections.heading: The big table

rows: Outer cases — on, at, open places

sections.body: Think of it as a 2 × 3 grid: **inside vs. on/at** × **being there vs. coming from vs. going to**.

sections.heading: Memory hooks
bullets: **-ss-** = in (inside): -ssa *in*, -sta *out of*.
**-ll-** = on / at: -lla *on/at*, -lta *off/from*, -lle *onto/to*.
**-a/-ä** endings = static (in, at)… **-ta/-tä** endings = movement away (from)… **-n, -lle** = movement towards (to).
The question words follow the same pattern: miSSÄ, miSTÄ, miHIN.

sections.heading: One word through all six
sections.note: Watch K-P-T: the endings -ssa, -sta, -lla, -lta, -lle close the syllable (weak: kaupassa, Helsingissä), but the illative keeps the strong grade (kauppaan, Helsinkiin). See [[kpt-nouns|K-P-T in nouns]].

sections.heading: Other uses of the 'outer' cases
bullets: **Having**: *Minulla on* — I have (adessive). See [[have-adessive|Minulla on]].
**Transport / instrument**: *bussilla, junalla, autolla, pyörällä, lentokoneella* — by bus, train… (adessive).
**Time**: *aamulla, illalla, yöllä, talvella, kesällä* — in the morning, in winter (adessive).
**Giving to someone**: *Annan kirjan äidille.* — I give the book to mother (allative).
**Feelings**: *Minulla on kylmä.* — I'm cold. *Se tuntuu hyvältä.* — It feels good (ablative).

topics.title: In, out of, into: -ssa, -sta, -Vn
topics.summary: Inessive -ssa (in), elative -sta (out of / from), illative -Vn (into / to) — for buildings, rooms, containers, towns and most countries.

sections.heading: Inessive -ssa/-ssä — in (Missä?)
sections.body: Weak grade + **-ssa/-ssä**.

examples.en: I live in London. I work in a hospital.
The milk is in the fridge.
The children are at school.
There are lots of cafés in Helsinki.

sections.heading: Elative -sta/-stä — out of, from (Mistä?)
sections.body: Weak grade + **-sta/-stä**. Also used for *from* (origin), *about* (topic) and with **pitää** (to like).

examples.en: I'm coming from the shop.
I'm from England.
I take the milk out of the fridge.
I like coffee. We're talking about the weather.

sections.heading: Illative -Vn / -hVn / -seen — into, to (Mihin?)
sections.body: Strong grade + the illative ending. See [[illative|How to form the illative]] for the three patterns.

examples.en: I'm going to the shop.
I'm travelling to Finland and Sweden.
I put the milk into the fridge.
We're going to Helsinki tomorrow.

topics.title: How to form the illative (into)
topics.summary: Three patterns: repeat the last vowel + n (taloon), h + vowel + n after a long vowel (maahan), -seen after a long e or in long words (huoneeseen).

sections.heading: Pattern 1: short vowel → double it + n
sections.body: Most words. Strong grade.

sections.heading: Pattern 2: one-syllable word with a long vowel or diphthong → h + vowel + n
Pattern 3: long vowel in a longer word → -seen

examples.en: I'm going home. (koti → kotiin; at home = kotona)
I'm going to work. (at work = töissä)
I'm going outside. (outside = ulkona)

topics.title: On, off, onto: -lla, -lta, -lle
topics.summary: Adessive -lla (on / at), ablative -lta (off / from), allative -lle (onto / to) — for surfaces, open places, people, transport and time.

sections.heading: The three endings

rows: Kirja on pöydällä. — The book is on the table.
Otan kirjan pöydältä. — I take the book off the table.
Laitan kirjan pöydälle. — I put the book on the table.

sections.note: All three take the **weak** grade: pöytä → pöydällä, katu → kadulla, ranta → rannalle.

sections.heading: When to use them
bullets: **Surfaces**: pöydällä, lattialla, seinällä, katolla, sohvalla.
**Open places / outdoor areas**: torilla, kadulla, pihalla, rannalla, kentällä, asemalla, mökillä, maalla (in the countryside), parvekkeella.
**Some towns and countries** — see [[place-names|-ssa or -lla with places]].
**People** (to have, give to, get from): *minulla, äidille, ystävältä*.
**Transport**: *bussilla, junalla, autolla, laivalla, pyörällä, jalan* (on foot).
**Time**: *aamulla, päivällä, illalla, yöllä; keväällä, kesällä, syksyllä, talvella; viikolla, tällä viikolla*.

examples.en: We're at the cottage the whole summer.
The children are playing in the yard.
How do you travel? — By train.
I'm coming from the market. I'm going to the station.
I'll call mum in the evening.

topics.title: -ssa or -lla? Places, towns and countries
topics.summary: Buildings and closed spaces take -ssa; open areas take -lla. Most towns and countries take -ssa, but some Finnish towns and a few countries take -lla.

sections.heading: Places in town
sections.note: Some places are idiomatic and just need learning: *postissa* (at the post office), *lääkärissä* (at the doctor's), *kampaajalla* (at the hairdresser's), *apteekissa* (at the pharmacy).

sections.heading: Countries and towns
bullets: **Countries and foreign cities**: almost always **-ssa**: Suomessa, Englannissa, Ruotsissa, Lontoossa, Pariisissa, Tukholmassa.
Exceptions with **-lla**: **Venäjällä** (Russia), and many islands: **Ahvenanmaalla** (Åland), **Kyproksella**, **Kanariansaarilla**, **Islannissa** is -ssa though.

**Finnish towns**: most take -ssa (Helsingissä, Turussa, Oulussa, Espoossa, Jyväskylässä, Lahdessa, Kuopiossa), but quite a few take **-lla**: **Tampereella, Rovaniemellä, Vantaalla, Imatralla, Seinäjoella**.
Rule of thumb: names ending in a landscape word like **-niemi, -joki, -vaara, -mäki** often take **-lla** (Rovaniemellä, Seinäjoella) — but always check, because many don't.

topics.title: Verbs of place and movement
topics.summary: Static verbs take Missä? forms, verbs of leaving take Mistä?, verbs of going take Mihin? — asua Helsingissä, tulla Helsingistä, mennä Helsinkiin.

sections.heading: Which case after which verb
sections.note: ✱ Finnish logic: *Jään kotiin.* (I stay home — 'into' home), *Löysin avaimen laukusta.* (I found the key in the bag — 'out of'). **käydä** uses Missä?: *Käyn kaupassa.* (I pop to the shop.)

examples.en: Where do you live? — We live in London.

examples.fi: Milloin te menette lomalle? — Menemme heinäkuussa Suomeen.
examples.en: When are you going on holiday? — We're going to Finland in July.

examples.fi: Lähden töistä kello viisi ja menen kotiin.
examples.en: I leave work at five and go home.

examples.fi: Ostan leipää kaupasta ja vihanneksia torilta.
examples.en: I buy bread from the shop and vegetables from the market.
The children come home from school.

topics.title: Postpositions: on, under, next to…
topics.summary: Words like päällä (on), alla (under), vieressä (next to) come after a noun in the genitive: pöydän alla — under the table.

sections.heading: Genitive + postposition
sections.body: Finnish puts these words **after** the noun (post-position), and the noun is in the **genitive** (-n).

examples.en: The cat is under the table.
The shop is next to the bank.
The car is in front of the house.

sections.heading: Missä? — Mistä? — Mihin? forms
sections.body: Most postpositions have three forms, just like the local cases: **-lla/-llä (where), -lta/-ltä (from), -lle (to)** — or -ssa/-sta/-en.

sections.heading: Examples from the course (kitchen & party pictures)

examples.fi: Missä lasit ovat? — Ne ovat kaapissa, lautasten vieressä.
examples.en: Where are the glasses? — In the cupboard, next to the plates.
The cat jumps onto the table.
I take the book from under the bed.
I'm going to my friend's place.

examples.fi: Lapset istuvat äidin ja isän välissä.
examples.en: The children sit between mum and dad.
The cinema is opposite the library.
Who are you sitting next to?

sections.heading: With pronouns
sections.body: Use the genitive pronoun, often with a possessive suffix in written Finnish: *minun vieressäni* (next to me), *sinun takanasi* (behind you), *hänen edessään* (in front of him/her). In speech: *mun vieressä*.

sections.heading: Prepositions (before the noun)
sections.body: A few words come *before* the noun and take the **partitive**: **ennen** (before) — *ennen joulua*; **ilman** (without) — *ilman sokeria*; **keskellä** can be both — *keskellä päivää*. **Kanssa** (with) is a postposition with the genitive: *ystävän kanssa*.

topics.title: Telling the time
topics.summary: Kello on kolme (It's three). Puoli neljä = half past three — 'half to four'! Varttia yli / vaille = quarter past / to.

sections.heading: What time is it?
sections.body: **Paljonko kello on?** or **Mitä kello on?** — Answer: **Kello on …** (the clock is …).
sections.tip: **puoli** + the NEXT hour: *puoli kaksi* = 1.30, not 2.30. This trips up every English speaker!

sections.heading: At what time? — Mihin aikaan? / Milloin?
sections.body: Use **kello** + time, or **-lta/-ltä** with the number in speech: *kello kahdeksalta* (at 8). With the hour on its own, just *kello kahdeksan* is fine.

examples.fi: Mihin aikaan sinä heräät? — Herään kello seitsemän.
examples.en: What time do you wake up? — At seven.
The course starts at half past six.

examples.fi: Kauppa on auki kello yhdeksästä kello kahteenkymmeneenyhteen.
examples.en: The shop is open from 9 to 21.
The train leaves at 14:25.

sections.heading: Official 24-hour time
sections.body: Timetables, opening hours and TV use the 24-hour clock read as two numbers: **14.30 = neljätoista kolmekymmentä**. Finnish writes a full stop between hours and minutes: 14.30.

topics.title: Days, dates and 'when'
topics.summary: maanantai → maanantaina (on Monday), maanantaisin (on Mondays). Dates use ordinal numbers: neljäs lokakuuta.

sections.heading: Days of the week (viikonpäivät)
sections.note: Days and months are written with a small letter. The -na/-nä ending is the **essive** case.

rows: tällä viikolla / ensi viikolla / viime viikolla

sections.heading: Dates
sections.body: **Monesko päivä tänään on?** (What's the date?) — Ordinal number + month in the **partitive** (-ta/-tä): *Tänään on neljäs lokakuuta.* (4 October). Written: 4.10.2026 (day.month.year).

examples.en: Today is Monday, 14 September.

examples.fi: Milloin sinulla on syntymäpäivä? — Kahdentenatoista toukokuuta.
examples.en: When is your birthday? — On the 12th of May (essive ordinal).
Christmas Eve is the 24th of December.

topics.title: Months and seasons
topics.summary: All months end in -kuu (moon): tammikuu, helmikuu… In January = tammikuussa. In winter = talvella.

sections.heading: Months (kuukaudet) — in … = -kuussa

rows: core month (heart of winter; tammi may also mean 'oak')

sections.note: Months use the **inessive** -ssa (in), and the elative/illative for ranges: *tammikuusta maaliskuuhun* — from January to March.

sections.heading: Seasons (vuodenajat) — in … = -lla/-llä
sections.note: Seasons use the **adessive** -lla/-llä. Note the stems: *kevät → keväällä*, *talvi → talvella*.

examples.fi: Milloin te menette lomalle? — Menemme lomalle heinäkuussa.
examples.en: When are you going on holiday? — In July.

examples.fi: Talvella Suomessa on kylmä ja paljon lunta.
examples.en: In winter it's cold in Finland and there's lots of snow.
In autumn there's lots of work at the cottage.

examples.fi: Kesällä aurinko paistaa koko yön Lapissa.
examples.en: In summer the sun shines all night in Lapland.
My birthday is in May.

topics.title: Talking about the weather
topics.summary: Millainen sää on? — Aurinko paistaa. Sataa lunta. On kylmä. Lämpötila on miinus viisi astetta.

examples.en: What's the weather like today?
What's the weather like in Helsinki?
How warm is it? / How many degrees below zero?

sections.heading: Weather expressions

rows: The sun is shining. / It's sunny.
On kymmenen astetta pakkasta. / On miinus kymmenen.

sections.note: Weather sentences have **no subject**: *Sataa.* (not 'it rains'), *On kylmä.* After numbers: **astetta** (partitive of aste, degree).

examples.fi: Helsingissä on pilvistä ja lämpötila on kolme astetta.
examples.en: In Helsinki it's cloudy and 3 degrees.

examples.fi: Rovaniemellä sataa lunta ja on viisitoista astetta pakkasta.
examples.en: In Rovaniemi it's snowing and −15 °C.

examples.fi: Huomenna tuulee ja sataa vettä koko päivän.
examples.en: Tomorrow it'll be windy and rain all day.
